clue.text: Wilde character whom Trollope's Violet Effingham becomes?

definitions.meaning: the wife of Sir Robert's friend in Wilde's play An Ideal Husband
in Trollope's Phineas Finn novels Violet Effingham marries Lord Chiltern and takes his title

explanation.walkthrough: One title links two Victorian books: Wilde's An Ideal Husband has a character of this name, and Trollope's heroine gains it by marrying Lord Chiltern.
explanation.definitionFit: The same aristocratic title names a figure in Wilde's comedy and the married rank Trollope's heroine attains.

clue.text: Party Going? or an unwritten Henry Green?

definitions.meaning: a party that is going is departing, read literally rather than as the title of Henry Green's novel
Green gave his novels one-word participle titles such as Living, Loving and Concluding, so this would fit the set

explanation.walkthrough: Party Going is a real Henry Green novel; read literally it means a group departing. His other titles (Living, Loving, Doting) suggest an imaginary sibling.
explanation.definitionFit: Departing is what a party going does, and the participle matches the pattern of Green's titles like Living and Loving.

clue.text: Runyon character in familiar Elmore Leonard setting

definitions.meaning: Nathan, the crap-game organiser in Damon Runyon's stories and Guys and Dolls
the Michigan motor city where many of Leonard's crime novels take place

explanation.definitionFit: Nathan of that surname runs the floating crap game in Runyon's world, and the Michigan city is Leonard's usual crime territory.

clue.text: Not usual, nor cliché, a play like Edward II

indicators.note: something not usual is out of its normal order, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A critic praises a fresh, unhackneyed play such as Marlowe's Edward II.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not usual' is the anagram signal. Marlowe's Edward II is a history play of the kind named after the chronicles of Holinshed and others it drew on.
explanation.definitionFit: Elizabethan history plays drawn from chronicles such as Holinshed's are known by this genre name, and Marlowe's Edward II is one.

clue.text: Unemployed fellow from the Universal

definitions.meaning: Samuel Johnson's essay series of this name first appeared in the weekly Universal Chronicle

explanation.walkthrough: Johnson's essays of 1758-60 appeared in the Universal Chronicle under this title, so the second half is a literary-history definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A loafer is a lazy fellow with no work, and Johnson's periodical essays in the Universal Chronicle bore that name.

clue.text: People like Anne Brontë's Helen Graham

definitions.text: People like Anne Brontë's Helen Graham

parts.words: People like Anne Brontë's Helen Graham
parts.note: Helen Graham is the mysterious occupant who rents Wildfell Hall in Anne Brontë's novel, its title naming her by that role

explanation.walkthrough: Anne Brontë's novel is The Tenant of Wildfell Hall: Helen Graham is the woman who rents the house, so people like her are renters.
explanation.definitionFit: Helen Graham rents Wildfell Hall, so those like her are occupiers who pay rent.

clue.text: Beaten by Forrest Reid?

parts.note: a withdrawal is something one beats, and the Belfast novelist Forrest Reid wrote a novel with that title

explanation.walkthrough: One 'beats' a withdrawal in the idiom, and Forrest Reid, the Belfast novelist, wrote a novel called The Retreat.
explanation.definitionFit: Forces beat a withdrawal in the idiom, and Forrest Reid's novel of 1936 bears that title.

clue.text: Equipage can't crash (unless those on board prove unreliable for their leader) (7, )

definitions.text: Equipage can't crash (unless those on board prove unreliable for their leader)

indicators.note: to crash is to smash to pieces, so these letters are broken up and reassembled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written; the apostrophe adds no letter

explanation.surface: A ship's commander insists his vessel cannot be wrecked unless the crew let him down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crash' rearranges EQUIPAGE CANT. In Herman Wouk's The Caine Mutiny the paranoid Queeg blames his crew's disloyalty, and they do relieve him of command.
explanation.definitionFit: Wouk's paranoid naval commander in The Caine Mutiny is convinced his officers are disloyal, and they finally take his ship from him.

clue.text: Laboured visionary poem is also art, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps suggests these letters could be arranged another way

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A critic finds an ambitious mystical poem heavy going, yet still a work of art.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges ALSO ART. Shelley's Alastor, or the Spirit of Solitude (1816) is the long visionary poem meant.
explanation.definitionFit: Shelley's long blank-verse work about a poet pursuing an ideal vision is often judged heavy and overwrought.

clue.text: "A children's writer should be, ideally, a dedicated semi-" (Joan Aiken)

definitions.text: "A children's writer should be, ideally, a dedicated semi-" (Joan Aiken)

parts.words: "A children's writer should be, ideally, a dedicated semi-" (Joan Aiken)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation: Joan Aiken, author of The Wolves of Willoughby Chase, ended the line with a word for a madman

explanation.walkthrough: Complete the quotation: Joan Aiken said a children's writer should ideally be a dedicated semi-lunatic.
explanation.definitionFit: Aiken's word for the half-mad devotion children's writing needs completes the hyphenated phrase as a term for a madman.

clue.text: Scandalous Bruce Lee case such a famous affair

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A notorious episode involving the martial-arts star Bruce Lee becomes a national sensation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scandalous' rearranges BRUCE LEE CASE into the French phrase for a notorious affair, the Dreyfus case being the classic example.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase names a controversial matter attracting wide public attention, like the Dreyfus scandal.

clue.text: Headgear for ballet suite?

definitions.meaning: Falla's ballet The Three-Cornered Hat (El sombrero de tres picos), known in French as Le Tricorne, with its orchestral suites

explanation.definitionFit: The cocked three-pointed hat gives its name to Falla's ballet, whose music is played as concert suites.

clue.text: Our dean composed formal poem

indicators.note: composed means put together, so these letters are assembled in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A college head writes a strictly structured piece of verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'composed' rearranges OUR DEAN into the French verse form with a refrain and only two rhymes.
explanation.definitionFit: A strict French verse form of thirteen or fifteen lines built on two rhymes with a repeated refrain.

clue.text: Part of Ode to Spring (otherwise known as Friihlingslied) may be pure gold ()

indicators.note: part of means only a section of the following words is taken, a run of letters inside them

explanation.surface: A fragment of a German spring song turns out to be precious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part of' takes the run inside SprING OTherwise. Frühlingslied is German for spring song; its spelling is mangled in the print but plays no part in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A cast bar of precious metal, often of pure gold, as held in bank vaults.

clue.text: Arch feature about an incarnation of Lawrence (and in French, both ways)

parts.note: C, short for circa, means about
T. E. Lawrence enlisted in the RAF under the name John Hume Ross
et is the French for and

indicators.note: both ways says the French word is read forwards and then backwards

parts.note: et again, the French for and

explanation.surface: An architect describes a detail of an arch, linked somehow to Lawrence of Arabia and French.
explanation.walkthrough: 'both ways' gives ET then TE, the French 'and' forwards and backwards. Lawrence of Arabia hid in the RAF as Ross.
explanation.definitionFit: In architecture this is a projecting ear or lug at the corner of an architrave or the shoulder of an arch stone.

clue.text: Every creative writer worth consideration, said Graham Greene, is given over to one

definitions.text: Every creative writer worth consideration, said Graham Greene, is given over to one

parts.words: Every creative writer worth consideration, said Graham Greene, is given over to one
parts.note: Greene held that any serious novelist is in the grip of a single fixed idea that drives all the work

explanation.walkthrough: Greene wrote in Why Do I Write? that every creative writer worth our consideration is a victim of one: a single ruling preoccupation.
explanation.definitionFit: A fixed preoccupation that dominates the mind, which Greene saw as the driving force of any serious writer.

clue.text: Some old writers making a point

definitions.text: Some old writers making a point

parts.words: Some old writers making a point
parts.note: writers here are the implements, not authors: feathers that had to be sharpened to a nib with a knife

explanation.walkthrough: 'writers' suggests authors arguing a point, but these are the writing implements, cut to a point before use.
explanation.definitionFit: Feather pens were the writing tools of earlier centuries, and each needed its nib cut to a sharp tip.

clue.text: Character unknown in French literature

parts.note: the French word for an unknown person, a stranger, also used of an anonymous figure in a story

explanation.walkthrough: The word is French for 'unknown', used as a noun for a stranger or anonymous person.
explanation.definitionFit: The French term for a stranger or person not known, an anonymous figure in fiction.

taken as written

clue.text: Man in French side is positivist ()

indicators.note: in places the abbreviation for man within the French word for side

parts.note: côte, close to côté, the French word for side or coast
M is the standard abbreviation for man

explanation.surface: A Frenchman on one team is a confident philosopher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts M inside COTE. Auguste Comte founded positivism, the doctrine that knowledge comes from observed facts.
explanation.definitionFit: Auguste Comte founded positivism, the philosophy that only scientifically observed facts give real knowledge.

clue.text: Another unwritten, and surely final, Henry Green?

definitions.text: Another unwritten, and surely final, Henry Green?

parts.words: Another unwritten, and surely final, Henry Green?
parts.note: Green's novels have participle titles such as Living, Loving and Concluding; an imaginary one meaning ending would surely be his last

explanation.walkthrough: Green's titles include Concluding and Nothing; an invented participle meaning 'ending' would fit the pattern and be fittingly his last book.
explanation.definitionFit: A participle meaning finishing or shutting down, suited as the title of a writer's last book.

clue.text: Chaps conceal roguish folk tale

indicators.note: conceal means one word is held inside another, hiding it

parts.note: chaps are men
arch means playfully roguish or mischievous

explanation.surface: Some fellows keep quiet about a mischievous story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'conceal' signals one word held inside another; 'roguish' as arch is the less familiar sense. The answer is German for a fairy or folk tale, as in the Brothers Grimm.
explanation.definitionFit: German Märchen are traditional fairy stories, like those gathered by the Brothers Grimm.
